basic_info.item_name: Pattern: AI assistant transparency and trust UX
basic_info.one_liner: How consumer AI analysis products earn CALIBRATED (not blind) trust: show each agent's reasoning, tool calls and cited evidence visibly, answer first and evidence second, label uncertainty honestly, and tie displayed trust to measured per-domain track records instead of usage-based scores.

needs.jobs_to_be_done: When an AI system analyzes their money, users' core jobs are: (1) UNDERSTAND - get a plain-language diagnosis of why the portfolio is losing, not just a verdict; (2) VERIFY - check AI claims against real, inspectable evidence (news items, prices, calculations) without redoing the whole analysis themselves; (3) CALIBRATE - learn where the AI is reliable vs. weak, per domain and over time, so they know when to rely and when to double-check (research shows people engage with an explanation only when scrutinizing it is EASIER than doing the task alone - Stanford HAI maze experiments); (4) STAY IN CONTROL - see what agents are doing, and be able to approve, correct, dismiss or defer; (5) DECIDE - convert the analysis into an actionable, risk-labeled next step (hold / trim / hedge / do nothing) they can defend to themselves.
needs.top_questions: 'Why exactly is my portfolio losing money right now - in one sentence?' 'Which agent said this, and what evidence did it use?' 'Can I see the original news / price / source myself?' 'How confident are you, and what would change your conclusion?' 'What did you just do while I was waiting?' 'Have calls like this been right before?' 'What are the risks of the suggested action, and what alternatives did you consider?' 'What happens if I do nothing?' 'Who is talking now, and why did another agent take over?'
needs.decision_drivers: Continued use is driven by: verified accuracy of past calls (a track record users can check); perceived evidence quality (cited, clickable sources vs. vague claims); cost of verification (hover-preview of the exact quote beats digging through documents); honest uncertainty handling (admits unknowns, scopes low-confidence claims); sense of control (can approve / modify / reject); and stakes-aware presentation - with money on the line, users pick verifiability over persuasiveness. Trust builds slowly and breaks quickly: one unexplained wrong 'confident' call or one fabricated-looking source costs more trust than ten good calls build.

pains.top_pains: (1) OVER-TRUST: AI overreliance - people accept AI recommendations even when wrong; classic XAI explanations often FAIL to reduce overreliance when the explanation is as complex as the task itself (Stanford HAI). (2) UNDER-TRUST: when transparency is absent or past errors were hidden, users micromanage every step or abandon the product. (3) Walls of unverifiable text and jargon that users skim, then blindly accept - worse than no explanation. (4) Theatrics: fake progress bars, fabricated confidence numbers, 'vanity trust levels' that rise with usage instead of accuracy (aiuxdesign.guide calls this a calibration lie). (5) Sycophancy: AI advice that overly affirms what the user already hopes (Stanford News, 2026) - especially damaging in a loss situation where users want reassurance. (6) Black-box multi-agent graphs: pretty node-and-edge visuals with no narrative of who concluded what from what.
pains.confusion_points: Finance jargon (DXY, drawdown, volatility, realized vs. unrealized P/L); unexplained handoffs between 5 agents ('who is analyzing now and why?'); bare confidence percentages with no referent ('70% of what?'); engineer-grade tool-call logs; knowledge-graph visualizations with too many nodes/edges and no summary sentence; multiple agents disagreeing with no visible synthesis or tie-breaking rule; Thai users additionally face English finance terms and English-only UI copy.
pains.trust_barriers: Black-box feel (no visible reasoning path from data to conclusion); missing, vague or dead citations, or hidden 'source unavailable' gaps; hallucinated or unverifiable sources; no track record of the AI's past advice; a wrong confident prediction with no follow-up or repair; fear of scams - strong among Thai retail users - amplified by marketing language, urgency tricks or anything that smells like a pump; unclear data provenance (which news outlet, which exchange, how fresh the data is).

ux.must_have_first_screen: Answer-first, evidence-second. In the first 5 seconds: (1) a plain-Thai one-sentence diagnosis of why the portfolio is losing (main driver + direction + rough magnitude); (2) the 2-3 key drivers as concrete numbers with a visible uncertainty label; (3) one-line 'what would change this conclusion'; (4) evidence chips on each claim (one tap to the source); (5) a quiet, non-theatrical agent status line (which cat agent is doing what, real steps). NOT first: a large agent graph, agent avatars animating, a wall of logs, or a verdict without reasons.
ux.workflow_preferences: Progressive disclosure in 3 layers: L1 conclusion (one screen, no jargon) -> L2 key evidence per claim (citation chips with hover/press preview quoting the exact passage) -> L3 full per-agent reasoning trace and tool-call log for power users. Multi-agent activity rendered as an inspectable timeline/ledger ('News Analyst fetched 12 items -> Risk Analyst flagged 2 conflicts') rather than a modal users must watch. High-stakes suggestions arrive as a decision card: What / Why / Risk / Alternatives + Approve / Modify / Reject / Defer. Group minor updates, interrupt only for genuinely high-stakes items ('never cry wolf'). Single page with anchored sections, mobile-first, deep links from every claim to its evidence.
ux.language_and_tone: Plain Thai at roughly an 8th-grade reading level (Microsoft HAX explicitly targets 8th-grade clarity); short sentences; consistent cat-agent names and fixed roles; numbers formatted with sign, baht and comparison ('+3.2% vs last week', '-8% vs your average cost'); every technical term glossed in one line on first use; confidence expressed as words + reason ('low confidence: the news contradicts itself') rather than bare percentages; the system must be allowed to say 'I don't know / the data is not enough'. No hedging walls, no marketing adjectives, no blame-the-user phrasing. [uncertain - Thai-specific reading-grade norms and preferred Thai finance vocabulary were not directly verified in this item; confirm with Thai user interviews]
ux.accessibility_notes: Body text >=16-18px for older shop customers; color-blind-safe gain/loss: pair green/red with arrows or +/- signs and position so color is never the only signal (Thai convention: green = up, red = down); text alternatives for agent states (screen-reader label: 'Risk Analyst: finished, 2 warnings'); touch targets >=44px and one-hand mobile use; a reduce-motion option for agent animations; visible keyboard focus on evidence chips and graph nodes.

design.implications_for_gold_assistant: Ten concrete recommendations for showing the 5 cat agents with calibrated trust: 1) ANSWER FIRST: open the page with the Lead Researcher's plain-Thai conclusion (why losing: driver + magnitude); evidence and agents below - never a graph or agent theater first. 2) PER-CLAIM CITATION CHIPS from each agent (headline+date, price series point, Fed/DXY data) with hover/press preview quoting the exact passage; deep-link to source; show broken/missing sources explicitly instead of hiding the gap (Shape of AI citations pattern). 3) MAKE EXPLANATIONS SIMPLER THAN THE TASK (Stanford HAI): instead of turn-by-turn reasoning text, highlight ON THE USER'S OWN CHART the moments that drove the diagnosis (buy date vs. price peak, the news-event marker) - verification by looking, not by reading logic. 4) UNCERTAINTY LABELS on every agent output: word + reason + 'what would change this'; low-confidence claims use scoped language and quieter visual weight; never show a bare 0-100% score without meaning. 5) PER-AGENT, PER-DOMAIN TRACK RECORD card: each cat keeps a small visible scorecard ('News-based calls: 6/10 right in the last 90 days') so trust tracks measured competence, not usage; update it after outcomes; show misses as well as hits (trust-calibration pattern). 6) VISIBLE HANDOFFS in the knowledge graph: tapping an edge shows 'News Analyst passed these 3 items to Risk Analyst because...'; the graph must be explorable FROM a narrative summary, not instead of one (multi-agent coordination UX). 7) AUTONOMY TIERS per action (Silent / Notify / Confirm / Escalate) published in an 'Agent Permissions' panel; portfolio-affecting suggestions default to Confirm/Escalate with a decision card (What/Why/Risk/Alternatives + Approve/Modify/Reject/Defer); irreversible actions are never silent (multi-agent autonomy-tier pattern). 8) HONEST PROGRESS: replace fake progress theatrics with a short real activity ledger of tool calls ('fetching SET news... 12 items... done') that can be collapsed; never invent steps, delays or confidence numbers. 9) SHOW DISAGREEMENT: let the Risk Analyst visibly dissent from Quant/Lead with a one-line 'dissent' chip - visible disagreement signals honesty and guards against sycophantic single-voice advice. 10) TRUST REPAIR FLOW: when a past AI call turns out wrong, surface it proactively in context ('our Oct 3 call was wrong because...'), explain what changed, and temporarily raise oversight prompts (trust builds slowly and breaks fast - repair must be proactive).
design.antipatterns_to_avoid: Fake progress bars or staged 'thinking' animations unrelated to real work; vanity trust/confidence scores that rise with usage instead of measured accuracy; one confident omniscient voice that never disagrees (sycophancy); a black-box agent graph with no narrative summary; wall-of-text explanations as complex as the underlying task; citation spam linking broad documents instead of exact passages; hiding broken sources or empty states behind filler; hiding all reasoning behind a chat bubble ('chat is not a transparency strategy'); jargon without gloss; urgency or social-pressure tricks ('experts are selling now!') that mimic the scam patterns Thai users fear.

Are Explanations a Solution?' - Stanford HAI - https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-overreliance-problem-are-explanations-solution ; (2) 'Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction' (18 guidelines, 4 phases: initially / during / when wrong / over time) - Microsoft Research - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/project/guidelines-for-human-ai-interaction/ and HAX Toolkit https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/haxtoolkit/ai-guidelines/ ; (3) HAX guidelines summary 'Microsoft HAI guidelines (HAX)' - AI Nerd Network - https://www.ainerdnetwork.com/learn/microsoft-hai-guidelines ; (4) 'UI/UX & Human-AI Interaction patterns' (multi-agent coordination, progressive disclosure, trust & transparency) - Agentic Design Guide - https://agentic-design.ai/patterns/ui-ux-patterns ; (5) 'Trust Calibration in AI - Meaning + UX Patterns for Appropriate Trust' - AI Design Patterns (aiuxdesign.guide) - https://www.aiuxdesign.guide/patterns/trust-calibration ; (6) 'AI UX Patterns | Citations' - Shape of AI - https://www.shapeof.ai/patterns/citations ; (7) 'Agentic AI and Multi-Agent UX Design Patterns' (autonomy tiers, decision cards, escalation design) - https://github.com/phazurlabs/ux-ui-mastery/blob/main/skills/agentic-ai-generative-ux/references/agentic-multi-agent-patterns.md . Consulted via search results only (titles/snippets, not fully read): CFI 'Explainable AI: Meaning and Why It Matters in Finance'; JIDMIS 'Explainable AI and Consumer Trust in Financial Services'; ScienceDirect (Computers in Human Behavior) 'Trust and reliance on AI - An experimental study on the extent and nature of overreliance'; Stanford News 'AI overly affirms users asking for personal advice' (2026); arXiv 'The Trust Calibration Maturity Model'; UXperiment 'Explainable AI UX: Design Patterns for Trust'; SAP Design System 'Explainable AI (XAI) - Building Explanations'. 10+ web searches run across: explainable AI in finance, agent transparency patterns, trust calibration / overreliance, multi-agent UI patterns, citation & evidence UI, progressive disclosure, Microsoft HAX.
evidence.confidence: medium - converging support from experimental research (Stanford overreliance experiments), validated industry guideline sets (Microsoft HAX, CHI 2019) and current agentic-UX pattern libraries (2024-2026); weaker on Thai-language specifics and on directly observed Thai gold-investor behavior, which this pattern item did not test with real users.
